paragraphs: The Fed held, but kept a December hike in play. On Oct 28, at Kevin Warsh's first meeting as chair, the FOMC kept rates at 3.75%-4.00% by a 10-2 vote; Governor Cook and Cleveland Fed President Hammack dissented in favor of a 25bp hike. Warsh said inflation is too high, that he is 'unwilling and unable' to call financial conditions tight, and that he would not pre-judge meetings. Futures moved to about an 85% chance of a hike at the Dec 8-9 meeting after the press conference (other snapshots put it at ~71-72%), up from ~71% at the Oct 24 pull. The data still runs hot: Q3 GDP grew 3.4% annualized (vs. 3.1% expected) and September PCE inflation was 3.6% y/y, core 3.1%, in line. The October jobs report is due this week (Fri Nov 6).

Yields fell anyway, on flight to safety. The 10-year rose to ~5.05% on Oct 28 after the presser, then fell to ~4.93% on Oct 30, its lowest close since Sept 9, about 7bp below the Oct 24 pull's ~4.99-5.00%. It fell about 36bp in October, its biggest monthly drop since December 2023. The 2-year fell to ~4.56-4.58%, so the curve steepened.

AI earnings broke tech again, and credit followed. Alphabet fell 12.6% on Oct 29 (its worst day since listing) and Intel ~29% on Oct 30, when the Nasdaq dropped 2.86% and the SOX over 7%. The Nasdaq lost 2.0% on the week and about 5% in October, while the equal-weight S&P 500 rose 4.9% for the month. HY spreads widened to 3.44% and IG to 0.94% on Oct 30 (FRED), both the widest in this dashboard's data. On Mon Nov 2 the Nasdaq fell another 1.07% as Marvell (-13%) and Lumentum (-18%) sank on their $115B merger and Oracle (-8%) announced a $20B stock-and-bond raise; the Dow rose 0.41% and most S&P 500 stocks gained. The VIX closed at 21.15.

Oil reversed hard. WTI closed Oct 30 at $104.12, its highest since mid-September, after gaining more than 15% in October. On Nov 2 Brent fell 7.6% to $104.77 and WTI 7.4% to $96.46 on U.S.-Iran peace-talk hopes and a reported Qatar-brokered plan to reopen Hormuz. That explains Monday's selloff in energy-services stocks and the rally in airlines. Gold fell to ~$3,899 on Oct 30 before recovering to ~$3,957 on Nov 2. Data note: Brent's Oct 30 close is reported as both $117.64 and $113.43, likely the expiring December vs. the January contract; Monday's 7.6% drop matches the $113.43 figure. FRED's Nov 2 yield and spread values had not posted on 11/02/26.

Rates fell on fear, not on data. The 10-year Treasury yield dropped about 19bp on Thu Oct 22 to ~4.95%, the biggest one-day fall since August 2025 and the first close under 5% since Sept 23, as money moved into bonds during that day's tech selloff. It ended Friday near 4.99%, down ~11bp on the week (third weekly decline) and below the ~5.10% at the Oct 18 pull. The Fed is in its blackout ahead of the Oct 27-28 FOMC. Odds of an October hike fell from ~15% to roughly 5-10%; a December hike is still priced at ~71%. The data didn't argue for a dovish turn. Jobless claims hit a three-month low (194K), Michigan's year-ahead inflation expectations rose to 4.7%, and the October flash PMI showed output prices rising at the fastest pace since August 2022. Housing is weak: the NAHB index hit 29 (lowest since 2012) and September starts fell 5.9%.

Equities: the chip losing streak ended Monday, but the AI trade broke down again Thursday. Meta fell ~7% after raising capex guidance to $135-145B, Lam Research ~9% on light guidance and Tesla ~3% after a 43% drop in Q3 net income. The SOX fell 6%+, the Nasdaq 2.6% and the S&P 500 1.21% (worst day since July), while the Dow was flat and the Russell 2000 rose. Friday the selling broadened: the Dow fell 1.23%. On the week the S&P 500 was -0.47% and the Nasdaq -0.71% (second straight weekly loss for both); the Dow was +0.41% and the Russell 2000 +2.0%, a rotation out of crowded AI names. The VIX closed at 19.45, below the Oct 16 intraday high of 22.31.

Credit and oil kept tightening the screws. HY spreads widened 13bp to 3.40% on Oct 22 (FRED), concentrated in AI-linked debt: Oracle 5-year CDS reached a record ~315bp on Oct 19, and long-dated Oracle, CoreWeave and Nvidia bonds trade well below par. Brent settled at $116.72 on Fri Oct 23 (six-month high, third weekly gain) and WTI at $103.27, after Houthi strikes on Saudi targets (including a claimed fire at Aramco's Yanbu facility) and Iranian claims of seven tankers hit in Hormuz, of which monitors confirmed two. Gold fell to ~$4,008.

Data note: FRED's WTI series is again out of line with reported settles. It shows $110.01 on Oct 19 and $107.89 on Oct 20, while reported settles were $103.66 and $101.79. The narrative above uses reported prices. Several CNBC and Bloomberg figures (Oracle/CoreWeave CDS, the PMI) were confirmed from search summaries because the pages blocked access; FRED's Oct 23 credit and yield values had not posted on 10/24/26.

newly_flagged.narrative: UPDATE (11/02/26): This flag now reflects Mon Nov 2: the Nasdaq fell 1.07% to 25,164.32 while the Dow rose 0.41% and the S&P 500 fell 0.51%, after the S&P had been up as much as 1.1% early. The drag was deal- and financing-driven tech: Marvell agreed to buy Lumentum in a ~$115B all-stock deal (4.5 Marvell shares per Lumentum share, closing expected 1H 2028), and Marvell fell ~13% and Lumentum ~18%, pulling optical peers such as Ciena down too; Oracle fell ~8% after announcing plans to sell $10B of stock and $10B of bonds to fund its AI buildout. Outside tech, about seven in ten S&P 500 stocks rose as Brent fell 7.6% to $104.77 and WTI 7.4% to $96.46 on renewed U.S.-Iran peace-talk hopes, lifting airlines, retailers and homebuilders. The October ISM manufacturing survey beat expectations with prices rising more slowly. Prior framing: The sign has flipped since this flag last fired: the Nasdaq Composite fell 2.15% on Friday Oct 16 to ~26,140, after closing at a record 27,599.79 on Oct 6. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 3.8% Oct 16 - its eighth straight losing session, the longest streak since 2008 - with AMD -5.95%, Intel -5.79%, Micron -5.63% and Broadcom -4.52% (Nvidia only -1.43%); the Nasdaq 100 fell 2.5% and tech lost over $1 trillion in value on the day. Coverage attributes the rout to a repricing of the AI capex cycle (BofA's Sebastian Raedler noted hyperscaler capex forecasts have tripled to ~$1 trillion and warned most past capital cycles 'ended in disappointment'), unwinding of crowded positions (AMD is down ~18.6% from its Oct 6 close), AI-debt stress (CoreWeave CDS hit distress levels on Oct 15), and the oil spike to $100+ WTI feeding inflation/rate-hike worries. This is a reversal of - not a continuation of - the Meta-Muse chip rally described below. Nasdaq rose 2.26% on Monday, Sept 21 to 27,122.09 - its first record-high close since June - outperforming the S&P 500 on the same combination of falling yields/oil and chip-sector strength described in the SP500 flag above. The semiconductor rally that Meta's Muse AI agent sparked on Sept 18 (Arm +13%, Intel +12%, AMD +9% that session, per multiple outlets) carried into Monday, when AMD crossed a $1T market cap for the first time; the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index notched its fifth straight session of gains.

The week of Oct 26-30 cost the Nasdaq 2.00% (to 25,437), with most of it on Fri Oct 30 (-2.86%, its worst day since June) after Intel fell ~29% on a weak Q4 revenue forecast and the SOX dropped over 7%. That followed Alphabet's -12.6% on Thu Oct 29 (its worst day since its 2004 listing) on weaker earnings, and Amazon's heavier AI-spending plans; coverage noted Alphabet, Microsoft, Amazon and Meta spent $201.9B on capex in the quarter vs. $175.5B of operating cash flow. The Nasdaq lost about 5% in October even as the equal-weight S&P 500 rose 4.9%, a rotation rather than a broad selloff. Monday Nov 2's -1.07% (Marvell-Lumentum deal, Oracle's $20B capital raise) extended the slide. The Fed's Oct 28 hold was not a driver: stocks rose slightly during Warsh's press conference. Prior framing: The 5-day window (through Fri Oct 16) is now -4.48%, the Nasdaq's worst week since late June, snapping a monthlong winning streak. The week's path: a hot September CPI on Wed Oct 14 (headline 3.7% y/y vs 3.6% expected, core 2.6% vs 2.5%; the 10-year yield rose to ~5.28% intraday) sent the Nasdaq and Russell 2000 down ~2% that day; Thursday Oct 15 the Nasdaq was flat (+0.08%) as investors rotated out of chips into other sectors and bonds (the 10-year fell back to 5.10%); and Friday's -2.15% chip/software rout finished the week. Chips have now fallen eight straight sessions (longest since 2008), with SOXX ~16% below its Oct 6 close. Drivers cited across coverage: AI-capex-cycle repricing, AI credit stress (CoreWeave CDS at distress levels), and oil above $100 feeding rate-hike fears - partly offset late in the week by Fed Chair Warsh declining to commit to an October hike. The 5-session window has rolled forward and now includes the Sept 22-23 pullback described in the DOW/RUSSELL2000 day-move flags above: Nasdaq set a second straight record close Tuesday Sept 22 (+0.4%) before falling roughly 1.1% Wednesday Sept 23 as the 10-year Treasury yield spiked to ~5.11% (highest since 2007) on hawkish Fed commentary and a hot PMI print. Even with that pullback, the index's 5-day change is still solidly positive at +3.67% (essentially unchanged from the +3.57% at last pull), because Monday's chip-sector record rally was large enough to absorb it. There is no genuinely new story here beyond what's already below - this reads as last week's rally holding up under a fresh bout of rate-driven selling, not being extended by a new catalyst. Nasdaq's 5-day change (Sept 15-21) turned solidly positive (+3.57%) even though the window contains the Sept 16 FOMC-hike selloff (Nasdaq -0.01% that day per the index data) - the index round-tripped and then broke higher on the Meta-Muse-triggered chip rally that began Sept 18 (Arm +13%, Intel +12%, AMD +9%) and continued through Monday Sept 21's broad rally (falling yields/oil, bitcoin above $85,000, AMD crossing a $1T market cap), which more than offset the FOMC-day losses within the same 5-day window.

The rate mechanism below ran in reverse: the Russell 2000 rose 1.65% on Tue Oct 20 as defensives and health care rallied, and it edged up 0.1% on Thu Oct 22 while the Nasdaq fell 2.6%, as the 10-year yield dropped ~19bp to ~4.95% and October-hike odds fell to ~10% (Bloomberg data put them near 5% by Oct 23). Most stocks rose on Thursday; the damage was concentrated in AI/semis. Friday's -0.29% was modest next to the Dow's -1.23%. Read: a rotation out of crowded AI trades into rate-sensitive small caps helped by lower yields, not a new small-cap-specific catalyst. Prior framing: The 5-day window through Fri Oct 16 is -3.05%. The rate-sensitivity mechanism below did show up on Wed Oct 14, when the hotter-than-expected September CPI (3.7% headline, 2.6% core) pushed the 10-year yield to ~5.28% intraday and briefly lifted CME odds of an Oct 27-28 hike to ~54%, sending the Russell 2000 down ~2% that day. Thursday's +1.38% bounce came as yields fell back to 5.10%, and Friday's -1.66% was driven more by the tech/AI-infra selloff than by rates. The Fed did not move this window (fed funds unchanged at 3.75%-4.00%); October-hike odds ended the week ~15% after Fed Chair Warsh declined to signal a move, though futures still price roughly one more quarter-point hike by December. The FOMC's Sept 16 hike (to 3.75%-4%, first since 2023) is the realization of the rate risk this flag was already tracking, and small-caps' higher rate sensitivity means they remain the most exposed index to it as the 10-year sits above 5%. Small caps are more rate-sensitive than large caps (higher average leverage, more floating-rate debt), so the run-up in the 10yr yield toward 5% on hot inflation data and hawkish Fed signaling has hit the Russell 2000 harder than large-cap indices over the past week. The same Middle East-driven oil spike also raises input costs disproportionately for smaller, less diversified companies.

Prior framing: The 5-day window (through Fri Oct 16) is now -4.48%, the Nasdaq's worst week since late June, snapping a monthlong winning streak. The week's path: a hot September CPI on Wed Oct 14 (headline 3.7% y/y vs 3.6% expected, core 2.6% vs 2.5%; the 10-year yield rose to ~5.28% intraday) sent the Nasdaq and Russell 2000 down ~2% that day; Thursday Oct 15 the Nasdaq was flat (+0.08%) as investors rotated out of chips into other sectors and bonds (the 10-year fell back to 5.10%); and Friday's -2.15% chip/software rout finished the week. Chips have now fallen eight straight sessions (longest since 2008), with SOXX ~16% below its Oct 6 close. Drivers cited across coverage: AI-capex-cycle repricing, AI credit stress (CoreWeave CDS at distress levels), and oil above $100 feeding rate-hike fears - partly offset late in the week by Fed Chair Warsh declining to commit to an October hike. The 5-session window has rolled forward and now includes the Sept 22-23 pullback described in the DOW/RUSSELL2000 day-move flags above: Nasdaq set a second straight record close Tuesday Sept 22 (+0.4%) before falling roughly 1.1% Wednesday Sept 23 as the 10-year Treasury yield spiked to ~5.11% (highest since 2007) on hawkish Fed commentary and a hot PMI print. Even with that pullback, the index's 5-day change is still solidly positive at +3.67% (essentially unchanged from the +3.57% at last pull), because Monday's chip-sector record rally was large enough to absorb it. There is no genuinely new story here beyond what's already below - this reads as last week's rally holding up under a fresh bout of rate-driven selling, not being extended by a new catalyst. Nasdaq's 5-day change (Sept 15-21) turned solidly positive (+3.57%) even though the window contains the Sept 16 FOMC-hike selloff (Nasdaq -0.01% that day per the index data) - the index round-tripped and then broke higher on the Meta-Muse-triggered chip rally that began Sept 18 (Arm +13%, Intel +12%, AMD +9%) and continued through Monday Sept 21's broad rally (falling yields/oil, bitcoin above $85,000, AMD crossing a $1T market cap), which more than offset the FOMC-day losses within the same 5-day window.
